title: Why Doesn't America Have More Small Cars?

Why Doesn't America Have More Small Cars?

# Why Doesn't America Have More Small Cars?

## America used to sell plenty of small cars. So why did SUVs and trucks take over the roads, nearly wiping small cars out in the process?

Photo by: Audi

Dan Mihalascu 

By: Dan Mihalascu

Oct 9, at 8:00am ET

Walk into a car dealership in Europe or Japan, and you can find tiny hatchbacks, narrow city cars, and compact models that seem almost perfectly suited to crowded streets. Walk into an American dealership... and the selection can look very different. Even the smallest vehicles on sale are increasingly dressed up as crossovers.

That's strange when you consider how useful a genuinely small car can be. They're easier to park, cheaper to fuel, and often less expensive to buy.

Yet the American market has spent decades moving in the opposite direction, with SUVs and pickups taking over showroom space once occupied by subcompacts and sedans. So why doesn't America have more small cars?

## Americans Really Do Buy Bigger Vehicles

The simplest answer is also one of the most important: Americans generally like bigger vehicles.

The US is a huge country, and many drivers routinely cover long distances on wide roads and high-speed highways. A larger vehicle can provide more interior space, a higher driving position, more cargo capacity, and a feeling of security in traffic.

There's also the practical reality of American households. A vehicle might need to carry several people, luggage, sports equipment, pets, or home-improvement supplies. A small hatchback can do many of those things, but an SUV often makes the job easier.

The market has responded accordingly. According to the EPA, trucks—including SUVs under federal regulatory classifications—accounted for 66 percent of new vehicles in the 2024 model year, compared with just 34 percent classified as cars.

And automakers follow the money. If buyers consistently choose a small SUV over a small sedan, there's a strong incentive to build the SUV.

## Small Cars Are Harder To Make Profitable

This is where the economics get interesting. A small car can be inexpensive for a customer, but that doesn't necessarily make it inexpensive for an automaker to develop and sell.

Modern vehicles need sophisticated safety systems, emissions equipment, electronics, infotainment, driver-assistance technology, and increasingly complex powertrains. Those costs don't shrink nearly as quickly as the vehicle itself.

A manufacturer might therefore make considerably more money selling a $35,000 compact SUV than a $22,000 subcompact hatchback, even if both require many of the same expensive technologies.

That helps explain why automakers have gradually abandoned some traditional small-car segments. Consumer Reports notes that several major brands have moved away from small cars while introducing hatchbacks and crossover-style vehicles with more SUV-inspired designs and interior space.

It's not simply that automakers don't want to sell small cars. They need enough customers willing to buy them at a price that makes the business worthwhile.

## Regulations Don't Make Tiny Cars Easy

Government regulations are another piece of the puzzle, although they're often oversimplified. A car sold in America has to meet U.S. safety and emissions requirements. That means an inexpensive little car designed for another market may need significant engineering changes before it can be sold here.

The problem becomes particularly obvious with ultra-small vehicles. Japan's famous kei cars, for example, are built around a completely different set of assumptions about size, power, roads, and urban transportation. Bringing one to the U.S. is not simply a matter of putting it on a ship and adding a sticker.

It may need different crash structures, safety equipment, lighting, emissions hardware, and other modifications. Those changes add cost and can undermine the very reason the tiny car exists in the first place.

Fuel-economy regulations have also influenced what automakers build. U.S. rules classify vehicles into different regulatory categories, and the country's CAFE system has historically treated passenger cars and light trucks differently. The latest federal rules are being recalibrated again, illustrating just how closely regulation and vehicle design are intertwined.

That doesn't mean regulations simply "killed small cars." Consumer demand remains a huge factor. But regulations can affect the relative cost and attractiveness of different vehicle types.

## Why Small SUVs Beat Small Cars

The biggest change wasn't Americans suddenly deciding that compact vehicles were terrible. It was automakers discovering that they could give buyers many of the benefits of a small car while packaging them as an SUV.

A small crossover can still be relatively easy to maneuver and fuel-efficient, but it offers a taller seating position, more cargo flexibility, and styling that many buyers prefer. That's an extremely powerful combination.

Instead of choosing between a tiny hatchback and a huge SUV, buyers can choose something in the middle. And once manufacturers realized how popular that formula was, the traditional small sedan and hatchback became increasingly difficult to justify.

There are plenty of reasons buyers prefer crossovers, including:

- Higher seating position: Many drivers like the visibility and easier entry.
- More cargo flexibility: A hatchback-style rear opening and folding seats are useful for everyday errands.
- SUV styling: Buyers often perceive crossovers as more modern or versatile than traditional small cars.
- Practical proportions: A small crossover can provide considerable interior space without being enormous.
- Perceived safety: Sitting higher and driving a larger vehicle can feel reassuring in traffic, even though vehicle safety is much more complicated than size alone.

The result is a strange middle ground: America still sells small vehicles, but many of them aren't marketed as small cars anymore.

## Some Drivers Want Small Cars Back

The online car community is frustrated by America's shift away from small cars. In r/whatcarshouldIbuy, commenters have lamented the disappearance of affordable compacts, while an r/cars thread argued that small cars make sense for buyers but are increasingly difficult for automakers to sell profitably.

The debate is not just about what Americans want, either. Another r/cars discussion questioned why small cars are disappearing, with commenters pointing to the growing popularity of crossovers and the economics of selling larger vehicles. A separate thread about Ford's push to bring back smaller cars showed just how much enthusiasm remains for compact vehicles.

## Could America Finally Get More Small Cars?

There are signs that the appetite for smaller vehicles is not completely gone. High vehicle prices and rising ownership costs can make affordability much more important. In 2026, some automakers have reported stronger demand for cheaper passenger cars and smaller SUVs as buyers become more price-conscious.

That doesn't necessarily mean America is about to become a nation of tiny hatchbacks. The SUV remains deeply entrenched, and American roads, regulations, and consumer preferences aren't suddenly becoming Japanese or European.

Comments

But there's an important distinction between small cars disappearing because nobody wants them and small cars disappearing because automakers can make more money selling something slightly larger. America actually has plenty of reasons to want smaller vehicles. They're efficient, affordable, easy to park, and perfectly adequate for millions of daily commutes.

The problem is that the American automotive market has created a powerful incentive to make those vehicles bigger, taller, and more expensive. So why doesn't America have more small cars? Because Americans have spent decades rewarding automakers for building something else. And until the economics—or the buyers—change significantly, the next small car is probably going to look a lot more like a small SUV.
